alt: A 900 kg rover on the Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg) has a weight of 8820 N, about 8800 N; on Mars (g = 3.7 N/kg) its weight is 3330 N, about 3300 N. The weight arrows are drawn to scale; the mass is 900 kg in both places.
caption: Mass stays the same; weight depends on the gravitational field strength.

alt: A 2.5 kg mass hangs from a newton meter reading 4.0 N on a newly explored moon, so g = 4.0 / 2.5 = 1.6 N/kg and a 70 kg astronaut there weighs 70 × 1.6 = 112 N, about 110 N. Near the Earth g = 9.8 N/kg, equivalent to a free-fall acceleration of 9.8 m/s².
caption: g = W/m: a force divided by a mass, in N/kg.

alt: A beam balance with an unknown object in one pan and standard masses in the other is level when their weights are equal; because both pans are in the same field, the masses are equal too, even on the Moon. A spring balance reads weight directly, so the same object gives a smaller reading on the Moon than on the Earth.
caption: A beam balance compares weights and so masses; a spring balance reads weight.

alt: Weight plotted against mass for 0.10 to 0.50 kg gives a straight line through the origin. A gradient triangle from the origin to 0.50 kg rises 4.9 N, so g = 4.9 ÷ 0.50 = 9.8 N/kg.
caption: Plot weight against mass in kilograms; the gradient is g.

after: ## Weight as the effect of a gravitational field (Extended only)
alt: Field lines point inwards from all directions to the centre of a planet. Objects on opposite sides have weight arrows pointing in opposite directions, each towards the centre. A satellite further away has a smaller weight, but not zero.
caption: Any mass in a gravitational field is pulled along the field with force W = mg.
